idiom_name: MIDDLEWARE entry: callable factory taking get_response
implementation_notes: Django ships the pattern as an onion: every entry in the MIDDLEWARE list is a factory that receives get_response and returns a callable taking the request, so a middleware runs its pre-processing, calls get_response(request) and post-processes the response - and returning without calling it short-circuits. The handler builds the chain once and applies it in list order for the request, reverse order for the response. Choose it when the concern needs Django's request, session or user objects.
code_sketch:
class TimingMiddleware:
    def __init__(self, get_response):            # once at startup: downstream chain injected
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):                 # per request
        t0 = time.perf_counter()                 # pre
        response = self.get_response(request)    # inner middleware or the view
        response['X-Time'] = f'{(time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000:.1f}ms'   # post
        return response
# MIDDLEWARE = ['django.middleware.security.SecurityMiddleware', 'app.TimingMiddleware', ...]
pitfalls: __init__ runs once at startup and __call__ once per request, so caching request data on the instance is a cross-request leak; use request attributes.
Order is semantic: AuthenticationMiddleware must follow SessionMiddleware, and a short-circuiting middleware stops everything below it, so moving an entry changes behaviour silently.
Exceptions propagate through response/exception hooks in reverse order, so error handling placed in middleware can hide the original traceback.

variants.name: WSGI middleware (PEP 3333)
variants.idiom_name: callable wrapping the WSGI application callable
variants.implementation_notes: PEP 3333 defines a server-agnostic shape: an application is a callable(environ, start_response) returning an iterable, and middleware is a callable that takes the wrapped application and returns another application, able to inspect or replace environ, wrap start_response and post-process the response iterable. This realization is independent of any framework and runs behind Flask/Werkzeug, Gunicorn or uWSGI, but it only sees the raw environment - so it is the right layer for encoding, compression, proxying and correlation IDs, and the wrong one for session or user logic.
pitfalls: Headers can only be changed inside start_response: once the status and headers are handed to the server, nothing can be appended.
The response iterable may be a one-shot generator: a filter that reads it must return a new iterable and call close() on the original, or the body is lost or the resources leak.
Under an async server the middleware runs per request on a thread from the pool, so blocking work still costs a pool slot - do not put CPU-heavy filters in the request path.
